note: Landmark papers, summarised by hand from the papers themselves. found = [label, value] pairs quoted from the paper unless marked. since = what later work did to the result. Every entry links to the original.

papers.t: Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud
papers.by: Henrietta S. Leavitt (communicated by Edward C. Pickering)
papers.one: A certain kind of pulsing star tells you its true brightness by how slowly it pulses, which turns it into a ruler for the universe.
papers.q: Leavitt had catalogued 1,777 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds from photographic plates. Did the ones that brighten and fade regularly follow any rule?
papers.how: She took 25 variables in the Small Magellanic Cloud and plotted each star's brightness against its period. Because the cloud is so far away, all 25 are at nearly the same distance from us, so differences in how bright they look are differences in how bright they are.
found: Brightness rises in a straight line with the logarithm of the period
papers.why: Measure the period of such a star anywhere, read off its true brightness, compare with how bright it looks, and you have its distance. Before this there was no way to measure distances beyond the nearest few hundred light-years.
papers.since: Hertzsprung calibrated the relation a year later. In 1923 Hubble found one of these stars in Andromeda and proved it was a separate galaxy. The relation is now called the Leavitt law, and it is still the first rung of the extragalactic distance ladder.

papers.t: Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation (The Field Equations of Gravitation)
papers.ref: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 844–847
papers.one: Gravity is not a force pulling across space; it is the shape of space and time, set by the matter and energy inside it.
papers.q: Newton's gravity acts instantly at any distance, which special relativity forbids. What replaces it, and can the replacement explain the small drift in Mercury's orbit that Newton's theory could not?
papers.how: Four papers in four weeks of November 1915. This last one, presented on 25 November, gives the final equations relating the curvature of spacetime to the energy and momentum it contains.
found: 43 arcseconds per century, reproduced exactly (paper of 18 November)
bent by 1.75 arcseconds, twice the Newtonian value
ten coupled equations, one line when written compactly
papers.why: Every modern result about black holes, gravitational waves, lensing, the expanding universe and the light-times on this site comes out of these equations.
papers.since: Tested for 110 years without a failure: light bending (1919), gravitational redshift, the binary pulsar, gravitational waves (2015), black hole shadows (2019). It is still not reconciled with quantum mechanics.

papers.t: A Determination of the Deflection of Light by the Sun's Gravitational Field, from Observations Made at the Total Eclipse of May 29, 1919
papers.by: F. W. Dyson, A. S. Eddington and C. Davidson
papers.ref: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 220, 291–333
papers.one: During an eclipse, stars near the Sun appeared slightly out of place, by the amount Einstein predicted.
papers.q: Does the Sun bend starlight, and if so by Newton's amount (0.87 arcseconds at the Sun's edge) or Einstein's (1.75)?
papers.how: Two expeditions photographed the Hyades cluster behind the eclipsed Sun on 29 May 1919, one from Sobral in Brazil and one from the island of Príncipe off West Africa, then compared the star positions with plates of the same field taken at night.
papers.why: It was the first new prediction of general relativity to be checked, and it made Einstein famous overnight.
papers.since: The result leaned on a small number of plates, and one Sobral instrument that gave a Newtonian-looking value was set aside for a focus problem; historians have argued over that choice. Radio measurements of quasars passing behind the Sun now confirm the bending to about one part in 10,000.

papers.t: A Relation between Distance and Radial Velocity among Extra-Galactic Nebulae
papers.ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 15, 168–173
papers.one: The farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us.
papers.q: Most galaxies show redshifted light, meaning they are receding. Does the speed depend on how far away they are?
papers.how: Hubble combined distances he had measured for 24 galaxies, mostly from Cepheid variables and bright stars, with velocities measured largely by Vesto Slipher and Milton Humason, and fitted a straight line.
papers.why: A straight line between distance and velocity is what an expanding universe looks like from the inside. Run it backwards and everything was once together.
papers.since: His distances were about seven times too small, so his slope was far too large. Georges Lemaître had derived the same relation in 1927; it is now the Hubble–Lemaître law. The modern value is 67 to 73 km/s per megaparsec, and the disagreement between methods is an open problem.

papers.t: Die Rotverschiebung von extragalaktischen Nebeln (The Redshift of Extragalactic Nebulae)
papers.one: The galaxies in the Coma Cluster move far too fast to be held together by the matter that shines.
papers.q: A cluster of galaxies should fly apart unless its gravity can hold its members. Is there enough mass in the Coma Cluster to do that?
papers.how: Zwicky took the measured velocities of galaxies in Coma, applied the virial theorem to work out how much mass is needed to bind them, and compared that with the mass implied by the cluster's light.
found: at least 1,500 to 2,000 km/s between members
the cluster needs roughly 400 times more mass than its light suggests
papers.why: This is the paper that introduced dunkle Materie, dark matter, as something that outweighs the stars.
papers.since: The factor of 400 was too high because distances were underestimated, but the conclusion held. Hot X-ray gas turned out to supply some of the missing mass; about 85% of the cluster's matter is still unseen.

papers.t: Energy Production in Stars
papers.one: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium, and this paper worked out exactly how.
papers.q: The Sun has shone steadily for billions of years. Which nuclear reactions can supply that much energy at the temperatures inside a star?
papers.how: Bethe went through every reaction between light nuclei that was physically possible, calculated how fast each would run at stellar temperatures, and eliminated all but two chains.
found: protons fusing directly, and a cycle that uses carbon and nitrogen as catalysts
four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus
papers.why: It explained why stars shine, why massive stars burn out quickly and where the energy for the main sequence comes from. Bethe received the 1967 Nobel Prize for it.
papers.since: Bethe thought the carbon cycle powered the Sun. In fact the direct proton chain supplies about 99% of the Sun's energy and the carbon cycle dominates only in heavier stars. Neutrinos from both have now been detected arriving from the Sun's core.

papers.t: The Structure of the Cloud of Comets Surrounding the Solar System and a Hypothesis Concerning its Origin
papers.ref: Bulletin of the Astronomical Institutes of the Netherlands 11, 91–110
papers.one: Long-period comets fall in from a vast shell of icy bodies that surrounds the Sun almost halfway to the nearest stars.
papers.q: Comets on very long orbits burn away after a few hundred passes, yet new ones keep arriving from every direction. Where do they come from?
papers.how: Oort took the 19 long-period comets whose original orbits were known most precisely and looked at how far out each had come from.
found: mostly 50,000 to 150,000 AU from the Sun
papers.why: It gave the Solar System an outer boundary a thousand times farther than Neptune, and a reservoir that explains every long-period comet.
papers.since: No object has ever been seen while in the Oort cloud; it is still inferred from the comets that fall out of it. Sedna, on a 11,400-year orbit, may belong to its inner edge.

papers.t: Dynamics of the Interplanetary Gas and Magnetic Fields
papers.one: The Sun's outer atmosphere is too hot to stay put, so it blows outward as a supersonic wind that fills the Solar System.
papers.q: Comet tails always point away from the Sun. Is the space between the planets static, or is something flowing through it?
papers.how: Parker showed mathematically that a million-degree corona cannot be held in by the Sun's gravity. The only stable solution is a continuous outflow that starts slowly and passes the speed of sound a few solar radii out.
found: a spiral, wound up by the Sun's rotation
a referee rejected it; the editor, Chandrasekhar, published it anyway
papers.why: The solar wind drives auroras and space weather, shapes every planet's magnetic environment and inflates the bubble that Voyager 1 left in 2012.
papers.since: Soviet and American probes measured the wind directly within four years. The spacecraft that now flies through the Sun's corona is named after Parker, the first NASA mission named for a living person.

papers.t: 3C 273: A Star-Like Object with Large Red-Shift
papers.one: A point of light that looked like a faint star turned out to be billions of light-years away and brighter than a whole galaxy.
papers.q: The radio source 3C 273 coincided with a star-like object whose spectrum had bright lines nobody could identify. What were they?
papers.how: Schmidt realised the lines were the ordinary pattern of hydrogen, all shifted toward the red by the same large factor.
found: hundreds of times the light of a large galaxy, from a region small enough to vary within months
papers.why: It was the first quasar. Nothing known could produce that much light from so small a volume, which led directly to the idea of matter falling into supermassive black holes.
papers.since: More than a million quasars are now catalogued. 3C 273 is still the brightest in the sky and the easiest for amateur telescopes: its light has been travelling for about 2 billion years.

papers.t: A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s
papers.by: Arno A. Penzias and Robert W. Wilson
papers.one: A radio antenna picked up a faint hiss coming equally from every direction in the sky: the afterglow of the Big Bang.
papers.q: A horn antenna at Bell Labs in New Jersey was noisier than it should have been. Where was the extra signal coming from?
papers.how: They accounted for every source of noise they could think of, including the atmosphere, the ground, the electronics and pigeon droppings in the horn. A residue remained.
found: about 600 words; the interpretation was left to a companion paper by Dicke's group
papers.why: A universe that began hot and dense should still be filled with cooled-down radiation. Finding it ended the debate with the steady-state theory.
papers.since: The temperature is now measured as 2.7255 K. Its tiny variations from place to place, first seen in 1992, are the most precise source of information about the universe's age and contents.

papers.t: Observation of a Rapidly Pulsating Radio Source
papers.by: A. Hewish, S. J. Bell, J. D. H. Pilkington, P. F. Scott and R. A. Collins
papers.one: Something in the sky was ticking every 1.337 seconds with the regularity of a clock.
papers.q: Graduate student Jocelyn Bell noticed a quarter-inch of 'scruff' on her chart recordings that returned at the same place in the sky each day. Was it interference, or a real source?
papers.how: A radio array covering two hectares near Cambridge, built to study the twinkling of quasars. Faster recordings resolved the scruff into evenly spaced pulses, and its position kept time with the stars and not with the Sun.
found: 1.3372795 seconds, steady to better than one part in ten million
outside the Solar System, inside the Galaxy
smaller than a planet, from the sharpness of the pulses
papers.why: Only something very small and very dense can pulse that fast. Pulsars turned out to be neutron stars, which had been predicted in 1934 and never seen.
papers.since: More than 3,500 pulsars are known. Hewish shared the 1974 Nobel Prize; Bell was not included, a decision still criticised. The best pulsars now serve as clocks that detect gravitational waves.

papers.t: Rotation of the Andromeda Nebula from a Spectroscopic Survey of Emission Regions
papers.by: Vera C. Rubin and W. Kent Ford Jr.
papers.one: Stars at the edge of the Andromeda galaxy orbit just as fast as stars near the middle, which they should not.
papers.q: In the Solar System, outer planets move more slowly than inner ones because most of the mass is at the centre. Does a galaxy's rotation fall off the same way?
papers.how: Ford had built an image-tube spectrograph sensitive enough to measure the velocities of faint glowing gas clouds far from the galaxy's centre. They measured 67 of them.
found: roughly constant all the way to the edge
papers.why: A flat rotation curve means mass keeps growing with radius long after the starlight has faded. Galaxies sit inside much larger halos of matter that does not shine.
papers.since: Rubin and Ford went on to find the same thing in dozens of spirals, and radio observations pushed it farther out. It remains the most direct everyday evidence for dark matter. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which began its sky survey in 2025, carries her name.

papers.t: Black Holes in Binary Systems. Observational Appearance
papers.by: N. I. Shakura and R. A. Sunyaev
papers.one: A black hole pulling gas from a companion star should be surrounded by a thin, bright, X-ray-hot disc, and here is what it would look like.
papers.q: A black hole emits nothing. If one is stripping gas from a neighbouring star, what would a telescope see?
papers.how: Gas with sideways motion cannot fall straight in; it settles into a disc and spirals inward only as friction carries its spin outward. Nobody knew what caused the friction, so they wrapped the ignorance into a single number, alpha, and solved the rest.
found: about 6% of the infalling mass for a non-rotating hole, far more than fusion's 0.7%
X-rays from the inner disc, ultraviolet and visible light farther out
the Eddington luminosity, where light pressure stops further infall
papers.why: The alpha disc became the standard model for accretion on to black holes, neutron stars, white dwarfs and forming stars. It is among the most cited papers in astrophysics.
papers.since: The friction turned out to be magnetic turbulence, identified in 1991. Thin-disc theory fails for holes that are fed very slowly, such as the one at the centre of the Milky Way.

papers.t: Discovery of a Pulsar in a Binary System
papers.by: R. A. Hulse and J. H. Taylor
papers.one: Two dead stars orbiting each other every eight hours gave physics a laboratory for testing gravity.
papers.q: A pulsar found at Arecibo in 1974 had a period that would not stay constant. Why?
papers.how: The period rose and fell on a regular cycle. That is the Doppler shift of a pulsar swinging around an unseen companion.
found: up to about 300 km/s, a thousandth of the speed of light
papers.why: General relativity says such a pair must lose energy as gravitational waves, so the orbit should shrink. Timing the pulses over the following years showed exactly that.
papers.since: The orbital period shortens by 76.5 microseconds a year, matching the prediction to 0.2%. It was the first evidence that gravitational waves exist, and earned the 1993 Nobel Prize. The two stars will merge in about 300 million years.

papers.t: Structure in the COBE Differential Microwave Radiometer First-Year Maps
papers.one: The afterglow of the Big Bang is not perfectly smooth: it has faint warm and cool patches, the seeds of every galaxy.
papers.q: If the early universe had been perfectly uniform, gravity would have had nothing to work on and no galaxies would exist. Are there ripples in the background radiation?
papers.how: The COBE satellite compared the temperature of pairs of points on the sky, 60 degrees apart, at three frequencies for a year, and subtracted the glow of the Milky Way.
found: 30 ± 5 millionths of a kelvin on 10-degree scales
nearly the same strength on all scales, as inflation predicts
papers.why: These are the density variations, seen 380,000 years after the Big Bang, that gravity later grew into galaxies and clusters.
papers.since: The WMAP and Planck satellites mapped the pattern at far finer resolution. Smoot and John Mather shared the 2006 Nobel Prize.

papers.t: A Planetary System around the Millisecond Pulsar PSR1257+12
papers.by: A. Wolszczan and D. A. Frail
papers.one: The first planets found outside the Solar System orbit the corpse of an exploded star.
papers.q: A pulsar's ticks should arrive with clockwork regularity. This one's arrived slightly early, then slightly late, in a repeating pattern. What was pulling on it?
papers.how: They timed the pulses at Arecibo for over a year and found two overlapping cycles, each the signature of a body tugging the pulsar back and forth.
papers.why: It proved planets exist around other stars, and in a place nobody expected them to survive.
papers.since: A third, Moon-mass planet was found in 1994. The two larger planets tug on each other exactly as predicted, which removed all doubt. Pulsar planets have turned out to be rare.

papers.t: Discovery of the Candidate Kuiper Belt Object 1992 QB1
papers.one: After five years of searching, a faint dot beyond Neptune showed that Pluto is not alone out there.
papers.q: Short-period comets seemed to need a source just beyond Neptune. Was the outer Solar System really empty apart from Pluto?
papers.how: They used one of the first large CCD cameras on a 2.2-metre telescope on Mauna Kea, taking repeated exposures and looking for anything that crept slowly against the stars.
found: magnitude 23, about six million times fainter than the eye can see
papers.why: It was the first of a whole population. The Kuiper belt reframed Pluto as the largest member of a class and eventually led to the 2006 decision on what counts as a planet.
papers.since: Several thousand Kuiper belt objects are now known. 1992 QB1 is officially named Albion. New Horizons flew past one, Arrokoth, in 2019.

papers.t: A Jupiter-Mass Companion to a Solar-Type Star
papers.one: A planet half the mass of Jupiter orbits a Sun-like star every four days, far closer than anyone thought a giant planet could be.
papers.q: Do ordinary stars like the Sun have planets?
papers.how: A planet makes its star wobble. They built a spectrograph able to see a star's velocity change by 13 metres per second and monitored 142 nearby stars.
found: 0.05 AU, an eighth of Mercury's distance from the Sun
papers.why: It was the first planet found around a star like our own, and it broke the assumption that other systems would resemble ours. Giant planets evidently migrate.
papers.since: More than 6,000 exoplanets are now confirmed. Mayor and Queloz shared the 2019 Nobel Prize.

papers.t: Observational Evidence from Supernovae for an Accelerating Universe and a Cosmological Constant
papers.by: Adam G. Riess and 19 co-authors (High-Z Supernova Search Team)
papers.one: The expansion of the universe is speeding up.
papers.q: Gravity should be slowing the expansion. By how much?
papers.how: A certain kind of exploding star always reaches nearly the same peak brightness, so how faint it looks gives its distance. They compared 16 distant ones with 34 nearby.
found: 10 to 15% farther away than they could be in a universe that is slowing down
99.7% or better that the expansion is accelerating
papers.why: Something with repulsive gravity makes up most of the energy in the universe. It was named dark energy, and nobody knows what it is.
papers.since: A rival team led by Saul Perlmutter found the same thing months later; Riess, Perlmutter and Brian Schmidt shared the 2011 Nobel Prize. Recent surveys hint that dark energy may be weakening with time, which is not settled.

papers.t: Galileo Magnetometer Measurements: A Stronger Case for a Subsurface Ocean at Europa
papers.one: Europa responds to Jupiter's magnetic field the way a ball of salt water would.
papers.q: Photographs of Europa's cracked ice suggested liquid beneath it. Could that be tested without drilling?
papers.how: Jupiter's tilted magnetic field sweeps over Europa and reverses direction every 5.6 hours. A conducting layer inside the moon would respond with a field of its own that flips in step. Galileo flew past in January 2000 at a time chosen to catch the opposite phase from earlier passes.
found: a global electrically conducting layer near the surface
salty liquid water; ice and rock conduct far too poorly
papers.why: It is the strongest single piece of evidence for an ocean inside Europa, holding about twice the water of all Earth's seas.
papers.since: The same method found oceans in Ganymede and Callisto. Europa Clipper, launched in October 2024 and due at Jupiter in 2030, carries a magnetometer to measure the ocean's depth and saltiness.

papers.t: Discovery of a Planetary-Sized Object in the Scattered Kuiper Belt
papers.by: M. E. Brown, C. A. Trujillo and D. L. Rabinowitz
papers.one: There is a world as big as Pluto three times farther out, which forced astronomers to decide what a planet is.
papers.q: A survey of the outer Solar System had found many large icy bodies. Was anything out there bigger than Pluto?
papers.how: A wide-field camera on a 1.2-metre telescope at Palomar photographed the same areas hours apart. Software flagged anything that moved; this object moved so slowly that it was missed until the images from October 2003 were reprocessed in January 2005.
found: at least as large as Pluto, from its brightness
papers.why: If Pluto was a planet, this was one too, and more would follow. The International Astronomical Union voted in 2006 to define the term, creating the class of dwarf planets.
papers.since: The object was named Eris, after the goddess of discord. It is slightly smaller than Pluto, 2,326 km against 2,377, but 27% more massive.

papers.t: A Direct Empirical Proof of the Existence of Dark Matter
papers.one: Two galaxy clusters collided, and their mass ended up in a different place from their gas.
papers.q: Maybe there is no dark matter and gravity simply works differently on large scales. Is there an observation that can tell the two ideas apart?
papers.how: In a cluster, most ordinary matter is hot gas. When two clusters pass through each other the gas clouds collide and stall while the galaxies fly on. They mapped the gas with X-rays and, separately, mapped where the mass is from the way it distorts background galaxies.
found: in the middle, between the two clusters
with the galaxies, ahead of the gas on both sides
papers.why: If gravity came only from visible matter, the mass map would follow the gas. It does not. Most of the mass is something that passed straight through the collision.
papers.since: Similar offsets have been found in other colliding clusters. Modified-gravity theories have not been able to reproduce the Bullet Cluster without adding some unseen matter of their own.

papers.t: A Bright Millisecond Radio Burst of Extragalactic Origin
papers.by: D. R. Lorimer, M. Bailes, M. A. McLaughlin, D. J. Narkevic and F. Crawford
papers.one: A single flash of radio waves, a few thousandths of a second long, arrived from far outside our galaxy.
papers.q: While searching old survey data for pulsars, an undergraduate found one enormous pulse that never repeated. Where did it come from?
papers.how: Radio waves are slowed slightly by the electrons they pass through, low frequencies more than high. The size of that delay tells you how much material lay along the path.
found: 24 August 2001, at the Parkes telescope; found in 2007
30 janskys, enough to saturate the receiver
far more than the Milky Way can cause, implying up to 3 billion light-years
papers.why: Whatever made it released in milliseconds as much energy as the Sun emits in days. It opened the field of fast radio bursts.
papers.since: Thousands are now detected each year. In 2020 a magnetar in our own galaxy produced one, so at least some come from highly magnetised neutron stars. Their delays are now used to weigh the gas between galaxies.

papers.t: Measuring Distance and Properties of the Milky Way's Central Supermassive Black Hole with Stellar Orbits
papers.one: Stars at the centre of the Milky Way whip around an invisible object four million times the mass of the Sun.
papers.q: What is at the exact centre of our galaxy?
papers.how: Twelve years of infrared images from the Keck telescopes, sharpened by adaptive optics, tracked individual stars as they moved. One star, S0-2, completed a full orbit during the study.
found: about 120 AU, at several thousand km/s
papers.why: That much mass inside a region that small cannot be anything but a black hole. It is the best evidence that supermassive black holes exist.
papers.since: Andrea Ghez and Reinhard Genzel, who led a rival group with the same result, shared the 2020 Nobel Prize. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the black hole's shadow in 2022.

papers.t: The Laniakea Supercluster of Galaxies
papers.by: R. Brent Tully, Hélène Courtois, Yehuda Hoffman and Daniel Pomarède
papers.one: Our galaxy belongs to a structure 520 million light-years across, defined by the direction everything in it is flowing.
papers.q: Galaxies cluster into filaments and sheets, but where does one supercluster end and the next begin?
papers.how: They measured distances to more than 8,000 galaxies, subtracted the cosmic expansion, and were left with each galaxy's own motion. Mapping those motions shows basins, like watersheds, in which everything drifts toward a common low point.
found: the Great Attractor, in the direction of Norma and Centaurus
papers.why: It replaced an arbitrary catalogue of clumps with a physical definition, and gave our place in the universe a name: Laniakea, Hawaiian for 'immeasurable heaven'.
papers.since: Laniakea is not bound together and will be pulled apart by cosmic expansion. A 2024 study suggested it may itself be part of a larger basin centred on the Shapley concentration.

papers.t: The Pluto System: Initial Results from Its Exploration by New Horizons
papers.by: S. A. Stern and the New Horizons team
papers.one: Pluto turned out to be geologically alive, with nitrogen glaciers, mountains of water ice and a hazy blue sky.
papers.q: What does a small, cold world four billion miles from the Sun actually look like?
papers.how: New Horizons flew through the Pluto system on 14 July 2015 at 14 km/s, after nine and a half years in flight. It passed 12,500 km above the surface and took sixteen months to send all its data home.
found: a heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice with no craters, so it is young
2 to 3 km high, made of water ice
about 10 millionths of Earth's pressure, with layered haze
papers.why: A world this small and cold was expected to be dead. Something is still resurfacing it, and no one predicted that.
papers.since: New Horizons went on to fly past Arrokoth on 1 January 2019 and is still returning data from more than 60 AU out.

papers.t: Evidence for a Distant Giant Planet in the Solar System
papers.by: Konstantin Batygin and Michael E. Brown
papers.one: The most distant known objects in the Solar System line up in a way that suggests an unseen planet is herding them.
papers.q: Six bodies with very long orbits all point in roughly the same direction and tilt the same way. Is that chance?
papers.how: They calculated the odds of the alignment arising by accident, then ran computer simulations to see what kind of unseen body would produce and maintain it.
found: elongated, some 700 AU out on average, opposite to the cluster
papers.why: If it exists, it is the first new planet found in the Solar System since 1846, and it was predicted the same way Neptune was.
papers.since: Nothing has been found. Critics argue that the alignment comes from where telescopes happened to look. The Vera Rubin Observatory's survey, which began in 2025, should either find the planet or the missing objects that dissolve the pattern.

papers.t: The Gaia Mission
papers.one: One spacecraft measured the positions, distances and motions of more than a billion stars.
papers.q: Until Gaia, accurate distances existed for about 100,000 stars, all close by. How do you survey the whole Galaxy?
papers.how: Gaia spun slowly at the L2 point, sweeping two telescopes set 106.5 degrees apart across the sky on to a single billion-pixel camera. Each star was seen about 70 times, and its tiny yearly shift as Earth orbits the Sun gives its distance.
found: more than 1 billion, about 1% of the Milky Way
24 millionths of an arcsecond for a magnitude-15 star, the width of a hair at 1,000 km
papers.why: Almost every distance inside the Milky Way used on this site, and in astronomy generally, now rests on Gaia.
papers.since: The third data release in 2022 held 1.8 billion sources. Gaia stopped observing in January 2025 and was switched off that March; its final catalogues are still being prepared.

papers.t: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger
papers.by: B. P. Abbott et al. (LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration)
papers.one: Two black holes collided 1.3 billion years ago, and the ripple in spacetime they made was felt on Earth.
papers.q: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916 and doubted they could ever be detected. Could they?
papers.how: Two detectors 3,000 km apart, in Louisiana and Washington State, each bounce a laser along a pair of 4 km arms. A passing wave stretches one arm and squeezes the other. On 14 September 2015 both saw the same signal 7 milliseconds apart.
found: 3 solar masses, in a fifth of a second
one part in a thousand billion billion, less than a thousandth of a proton's width
papers.why: It was the first direct detection of gravitational waves, the first observation of black holes merging, and the start of astronomy without light.
papers.since: Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize. Several hundred mergers have now been catalogued, including one of neutron stars in 2017 that was also seen in light.

papers.t: A Brief Visit from a Red and Extremely Elongated Interstellar Asteroid
papers.one: The first object ever seen passing through the Solar System from another star was long, red and already leaving.
papers.q: An object found on 19 October 2017 was moving too fast to be bound to the Sun. What was it?
papers.how: Telescopes in Hawaii and Chile followed it for the ten days before it faded, measuring its path, colour and the way its brightness changed as it tumbled.
found: a factor of ten every 7.3 hours, so one axis is about ten times longer than another
papers.why: Every planetary system should throw out debris as it forms. This was the first piece of someone else's.
papers.since: It was named 1I/ʻOumuamua. It sped up slightly as it left, with no visible outgassing, which is still argued over. Two more interstellar visitors have followed: the comets 2I/Borisov in 2019 and 3I/ATLAS in 2025.

papers.t: Cassini Finds Molecular Hydrogen in the Enceladus Plume: Evidence for Hydrothermal Processes
papers.one: The ocean inside Saturn's moon Enceladus contains the chemical fuel that microbes on Earth live on.
papers.q: Enceladus sprays its ocean into space through cracks at its south pole. Is there an energy source down there that life could use?
papers.how: On 28 October 2015 Cassini flew through the plume 49 km above the surface with its mass spectrometer open, sampling the gas directly.
found: Most likely source of the hydrogen
hot water reacting with rock on the sea floor
papers.why: Hydrogen and carbon dioxide together are food for methane-producing microbes. Enceladus has liquid water, organic molecules and now a source of chemical energy: the three things life as we know it needs.
papers.since: Phosphorus, the last of the six key elements, was found in plume grains in 2023. No mission to return there is yet approved.

papers.t: First M87 Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole
papers.one: The first picture of a black hole: a dark centre ringed by light bent around it.
papers.q: General relativity predicts that a black hole lit by surrounding gas should show a dark 'shadow' of a specific size. Can it be seen?
papers.how: Eight radio telescopes on four continents observed together in April 2017, synchronised by atomic clocks, forming a virtual dish the size of the Earth. The recordings were flown to two supercomputers on hard drives.
found: 42 ± 3 millionths of an arcsecond, an orange on the Moon
brighter on one side, as expected for gas orbiting near the speed of light
papers.why: It turned black holes from an inference into something photographed, and the shadow's size matched Einstein's prediction.
papers.since: Polarised images in 2021 mapped the magnetic fields near the horizon. The same team imaged the Milky Way's own black hole in 2022.

papers.t: Planck 2018 Results. VI. Cosmological Parameters
papers.one: The whole observable universe is described by six numbers, and this paper measures them to about one per cent.
papers.q: How old is the universe, what is it made of and how fast is it expanding?
papers.how: The Planck satellite mapped the temperature and polarisation of the cosmic microwave background over the whole sky from 2009 to 2013. The sizes of the hot and cold patches depend on the universe's contents and geometry.
papers.why: These are the numbers this site uses to turn a redshift into a distance and a light-travel time.
papers.since: Measurements of the expansion rate from nearby supernovae give about 73, not 67. The gap, called the Hubble tension, has grown more significant and is not explained.

papers.t: First Sagittarius A* Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole in the Center of the Milky Way
papers.one: A picture of the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy.
papers.q: Stellar orbits had weighed the object at the galactic centre. Does it look like a black hole?
papers.how: The same April 2017 campaign that imaged M87. This target is a thousand times smaller and a thousand times closer, so it appears about the same size, but the gas around it circles in minutes and the picture changes while it is being taken.
found: a black hole of 4 million solar masses, as the stellar orbits require
papers.why: Two black holes differing in mass by a factor of 1,500 produce the same ring, scaled as general relativity says it should be.
papers.since: A polarised image in 2024 showed ordered magnetic fields spiralling around the hole, much like M87's.

papers.t: Successful Kinetic Impact into an Asteroid for Planetary Defence
papers.by: R. Terik Daly and the DART team
papers.one: A spacecraft was flown into an asteroid on purpose, and it worked.
papers.q: If an asteroid were found on course for Earth, could a spacecraft hit something that small, that far away, with no one steering?
papers.how: DART navigated itself for the final four hours using its own camera. Its target was Dimorphos, a 150-metre moon of the asteroid Didymos, chosen because a change in the moon's orbit could be timed from Earth.
found: shortened by 33 minutes, from 11 h 55 min (companion paper, Thomas et al.)
papers.why: It was the first time humanity deliberately changed the motion of a celestial body. Debris thrown off by the impact gave several times more push than the spacecraft alone.
papers.since: ESA's Hera spacecraft was due to arrive in November 2026 to measure the crater and the moon's mass.

papers.t: The NANOGrav 15 yr Data Set: Evidence for a Gravitational-wave Background
papers.one: The whole galaxy is gently rising and falling on gravitational waves light-years long.
papers.q: Pairs of supermassive black holes should fill the universe with very slow gravitational waves. Is there a detector big enough?
papers.how: They timed 67 millisecond pulsars for 15 years. A passing wave makes pulses from one direction arrive early and from another late, in a specific pattern across the sky that depends on the angle between each pair of pulsars.
found: 3 to 4 sigma: strong evidence, short of a formal detection
papers.why: It opens a second window on gravitational waves, at frequencies ten billion times lower than LIGO's.
papers.since: European, Indian, Australian and Chinese pulsar-timing teams reported consistent signals on the same day. The source is not yet identified.

papers.t: Spectroscopic Confirmation of Two Luminous Galaxies at a Redshift of 14
papers.by: Stefano Carniani and the JADES collaboration
papers.one: Two bright galaxies already existed less than 300 million years after the Big Bang.
papers.q: Webb's images kept turning up galaxies that looked too bright, too early. Were they really that far away?
papers.how: A colour alone can mislead. They spread each galaxy's light into a spectrum with Webb's NIRSpec instrument for nearly ten hours and found the sharp cut-off that hydrogen imposes, which pins down the redshift.
papers.why: Galaxies this bright this early were not predicted. Either stars formed faster in the young universe than models assume, or something else is making these galaxies shine.
papers.since: Oxygen was detected in the brighter galaxy in 2025, which refined its redshift to 14.18 and means at least one generation of stars had already lived and died. A galaxy at 14.44 was reported the same year.
